title: Sequenced tool pipelines with injection validation and loop guards
creator: Asha Kapoor
description:
Goal: implement a robust sequenced tool-execution pipeline in the Core API that supports multi-tool chaining, deterministic tool-result injection into model contexts, streaming responses while tools execute, structured-output enforcement, and recursion/loop protections. This ticket covers the design and implementation of the execution controller, deterministic injection strategy, guard heuristics to prevent runaway recursion, and the API compatibility layer so existing SDKs and older models can opt-in without breaking behavior.

Background: Our hosted API and Dedicated runtimes already allow single-step tool calls and basic streaming. Customers have begun authoring multi-step tool pipelines (e.g., info retrieval -> transform -> external side-effect) and want consistent semantics: injected tool outputs must be schema-validated, injected at predictable positions in the prompt/KV cache, and not cause infinite loops when tools call back into the executor (directly or via the model). Existing tickets (ENG-14200, ENG-15121) explored kernel-level scheduling and streaming improvements; this ticket implements the execution loop contract and safety checks.

Success criteria / Acceptance Criteria: 
- Core API exposes a stable execution controller option: pipeline_mode="sequenced" with documented semantics.
- Tool-result injection: each tool's output is wrapped with a structured envelope and validated against declared JSON schema (or simple type contract). Invalid tool outputs are rejected with a well-defined error path and fallback to the previous model prompt state.
- Streaming semantics: partial model tokens may be streamed to the client while background tools run; tool outputs that arrive mid-stream are injected atomically at the next safe token boundary.
- Loop/recursion guards: controller enforces a configurable max-invocations-per-request (default=5) and detects repeated state patterns (same request signature + same tool sequence) to halt and return a clear error.
- Backwards compatibility: old SDKs default to current behavior; new clients can opt-in to sequenced pipelines; server logs include an upgrade warning if an older client requests pipeline features.
- Tests: integration tests for multi-tool happy path, schema-violation path, streaming-injection path, and loop-guard path. Performance regression <5% p99 latency for typical single-tool requests.

Design notes and trade-offs: 
- Deterministic injection position: we place injected tool results into the KV-cache as a named segment and also append a small assistant turn in the user-visible prompt history. This makes replay and caching decisions simpler, but slightly increases prompt size.
- Schema validation: use a minimal, fast validator (subset of JSON Schema) enforced in the execution controller. Full JSON Schema is too heavy for hot-path validation. Customers needing complex schemas can pre-validate in the tool.
- Streaming integration: to avoid re-entrancy complexity, we add a token-boundary semaphore: the stream flushes buffered tokens to the client and pauses the model streaming while the next tool injection is applied; the pause must be bounded (default 200ms) to keep latency SLO reasonable.
- Loop detection: combine a simple invocation counter + request-signature hash window (sliding set of last 8 signatures). This is not a perfect halting oracle but prevents common accidental loops and malicious recursive constructs.

Implementation plan: 
1) Controller API + config flags (2d) 
2) Lightweight schema validator and envelope format (2d)
3) Streaming edge: token-boundary semaphore and pause logic (3d)
4) Loop guard heuristics + metrics (2d)
5) Integration tests + perf benchmarks (3d)
6) Docs + SDK compatibility notes (1d)

Rollout plan: feature-flag on runtime-1.24 behind ff.sequenced_pipelines. Beta for Dedicated customers and internal Redwood dev teams for 1 week. Monitor error rates, latency p50/p95/p99, and loop-guard activations.

Docs/PRs/Artifacts: 
- Draft design doc: https://docs.internal.redwood.ai/seq-tool-pipelines (internal)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2387
- Perf dashboard (internal): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/seq-pipelines

Open questions: 
- Should the default max-invocations-per-request be 5 or 3? Ops/PM leaning to 5 for flexibility; security prefers 3.
- Schema validator language: subset of JSON Schema vs. custom YAML contract.

Notes for reviewers: pay attention to stream pause latencies and client-sdk ergonomics for partial outputs. The controller must reject any tool that declares "side_effect=write_disk" unless caller is in a dedicated/private deployment with appropriate policy.
acceptance_criteria: tool outputs wrapped in structured envelope and validated against declared contract
partial streaming supported; tool injection occurs at safe token boundaries
loop guard enforces default max-invocations-per-request and halts repeated signatures
performance regression <5% p99 for single-tool requests
